summary: We developed KalaApi, a web app that turns 25 years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspots into one comparable burning calendar for Indonesia: the nation, 38 provinces, 383 kabupaten, or any circle or box a user draws. Raw hotspot counts jump 6.5 times in 2012 when VIIRS starts, mostly because the new sensor sees more small fires. KalaApi counts fire-days on a 0.05° grid and converts pre-2012 MODIS records to VIIRS-equivalent values with a measured, activity-dependent fit; after harmonization the jump is 1.2 times. A disaster officer can see when an area usually burns and whether this month is unusual against its 2001-2025 median. We tested it on held-out years (national error +1.8% and +3.2%) and against official burned area per province (225 province-years, log r = 0.81). S-NPP VIIRS ended on 2 Nov 2026, so a provisional NOAA-20 layer continues the view to 14 Nov. Every error is published on the Method page.
details:
The problem. In 2015, fires in Indonesia burned 2.6 million hectares by the official estimate, and one Sentinel-1 radar study (Lohberger et al. 2018) found 4.6 million. A disaster agency (BPBD) preparing for the next season needs to know: when does my area usually burn, and is this year unusual? The satellite record cannot answer that today. MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) see fires differently, so raw hotspot counts jump 6.5 times in 2012. Any trend or "worst year" comparison across that line is mostly the sensor change.

What KalaApi does.
• A burning-activity calendar from 2001 to 2 Nov 2026 for the nation, 38 provinces and 383 kabupaten: one row per year, one column per month (or per week). Pre-2012 rows are marked as estimates.
• "This month vs history": for example, Central Kalimantan in October 2026 had 4,580 fire-days against a 2001-2025 October median of 1,422 (x3.22, 80th percentile).
• The typical start, peak and end of the fire season, and whether this year's season started early or late.
• A custom area: enter a point and a radius, pick a date range, and get the same 25-year month calendar, an "is this period unusual?" tile, and a cell-by-week CSV.
• Weeks flagged as elevated (90th percentile) or extreme (97.5th), with a "low base" label where a high percentile means only a few fire-days.
• Peat-only and mineral-soil-only views, a comparison of two places, a printable one-page brief for BPBD, and CSV and PNG downloads. Everything is in Bahasa Indonesia and English.

How the harmonization works. A fire-day is one 0.05-degree cell (about 5.5 km) on one day with at least one daytime detection (MODIS confidence 30 or more, VIIRS nominal or high, vegetation fires only). Counting cells instead of hotspots removes most of the 375 m vs 1 km resolution difference. VIIRS still sees small fires that MODIS misses, so the VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio falls as fire activity rises. For each stratum (a province or island group, split into peat and mineral soil) we fit weekly VIIRS fire-days as V = alpha x M^b over the 2012-2026 overlap (shared b = 0.875). Before 2012 the series is this back-cast, with a 90% bootstrap band. From 2012 it is observed S-NPP VIIRS.

How we checked it.
• Holdout years 2019 and 2023 (calibrated without them): national annual error +1.8% and +3.2%; 80% of province-years within 20%; median weekly correlation 0.90.
• A reverse test (calibrate on 2018-2026, predict 2012-2017): 84% of province-years within 20%.
• Yearly national fire-days rank 2015-2025 like official burned area (SiPongi, as reproduced by GoodStats): Spearman 0.90, n = 11.
• Against official burned area per province (SiPongi KEMENHUT, 2018-2024, 225 province-years): log r = 0.81. Tested within each province, the median Spearman is 0.75 (27 of 31 provinces positive). It does not hold in East and West Nusa Tenggara (savanna and grass fires).
• Why not one fixed ratio: in the same holdouts, 80% (2019/2023) and 84% (2012-2017) of province-years fall within ±20% with the activity-dependent fit, against 71% and 72% with a fixed ratio (b = 1). The fixed ratio is closer on some national totals, so the gain is at province level.
• Flags do not depend on the back-cast: recomputing every weekly percentile with observed VIIRS only (2012-2025) gives a rank correlation of 0.94 with the main baseline.
• A bridge from NOAA-20 to S-NPP (to continue after S-NPP ended) was tested: 96% of province-years within 20%, but national error reached 12.5% in some years, so we have not merged it yet.
• The Method page answers nine questions a remote-sensing scientist will ask, including why Central Kalimantan 2006 ranks above 2015 and how we corrected the El Nino analysis for multiple testing (288 of 422 areas pass FDR q < 0.05; exploratory only).

Limits. Hotspots are heat detections, not burned area. Clouds and thick haze hide some fires. Pre-2012 values are estimates. Small areas are noisy. The peat map is a 30 m global map, not the official KLHK layer. KalaApi is not an official product and does not forecast.

Why now. S-NPP VIIRS stopped delivering data on 2 Nov 2026, and NASA plans to retire Terra and Aqua MODIS in 2027. Without a calibrated bridge, 25 years of fire history become hard to compare with what comes next.

Who it is for. BPBD officers and provincial fire task forces, peatland restoration teams, and researchers who need a consistent fire history. We have not yet tested KalaApi with a BPBD. That is our next step.

Tools. Python (pandas, numpy) for the pipeline; TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS and Apache ECharts for the web app; GitHub Pages for hosting. Code: https://github.com/6-Scrambled-Eggs/KalaApi

Use of AI. We built KalaApi with AI assistance. Claude (Anthropic) helped write the Python pipeline, the web app, tests and documentation, and helped plan the method and review results. The team chose the challenge, set the requirements, and reviewed the code and every published number. No NASA logos appear in AI-made content.
